The House finch (Haemorhous mexicanus) is a small passerine whose life history has been characterized through both captive and field studies. Eggs incubated under controlled laboratory conditions at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] typically complete embryonic development and hatch after 14 days [ab = 14 days], an incubation period that aligns with values documented for other cardueline finches. Newly hatched nestlings emerge with a modest wet weight at birth of 1.3 grams [Wwb = 1.3 grams], a mass that reflects the altricial developmental mode common among passerines. This initial body mass is notably low compared to the ultimate wet weight of adults, which reaches approximately 26.1 grams [Wwi = approximately 26.1 grams] under favorable nutritional conditions, representing a roughly twentyfold increase over the course of the nestling and fledgling period. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg itself, preceding any embryonic development, has been recorded at 1.95 grams [Ww0 = 1.95 grams], indicating that the yolk and albumen constitute a substantial maternal investment relative to the neonate's size.

Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolism during the breeding season, which center around a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the developmental trajectory of nestlings proceeds along a predictable schedule. Fledging, defined as the achievement of the first sustained flight and departure from the nest, occurs at 16 days after hatching [tx = 16 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is characteristic of species that face high predation pressure on the nest and reflects a trade-off between rapid feather development and the attainment of sufficient neuromuscular coordination for flight. Following fledging, the young birds enter a prolonged period of parental dependency during which they continue to refine their foraging skills and gradually achieve nutritional independence. The time since birth at fledging represents a critical developmental milestone, after which the juveniles begin to explore habitats beyond the immediate vicinity of the natal site, though they typically remain within the parental territory for several additional weeks.

Sexual maturation in the House finch follows a distinctly different timescale from the rapid early growth phase. Puberty, marked by the onset of gonadal development and the emergence of sexually dimorphic plumage characteristics, is reached at 48 days since birth [tp = 48 days since birth] under captive conditions maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of reproductive potential is notable among North American finches and allows first-year birds to participate in breeding during the same season in which they were hatched, provided that environmental conditions and food availability are favorable. The onset of gametogenesis and the accompanying surge in circulating testosterone in males, or estradiol in females, triggers the development of the bright carotenoid-based plumage that is so characteristic of the species and that plays a central role in mate attraction and social signaling within breeding aggregations.

Despite the early achievement of sexual maturity, first reproduction in the House finch is often deferred until the following breeding season in many populations. The first successful brood is typically initiated at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth] under the thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that characterizes the active metabolic period. This delay between the attainment of puberty and the first breeding attempt is thought to reflect the time required for young birds to establish a breeding territory, secure a mate, and accumulate sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The reproductive effort itself is considerable, with females laying four eggs per clutch [N_R_i = four eggs per clutch] and producing multiple broods across the breeding season, a pattern that is facilitated by the relatively long breeding window available in the species' predominantly temperate and subtropical range.

The species exhibits a maximum lifespan that underscores its position along the slow-fast continuum of passerine life histories. The oldest documented individuals in wild populations have been recorded at approximately 11.6 years [am = approximately 11.6 years], a value that reflects the species' position among longer-lived small passerines at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Field records indicate that females typically produce about three clutches annually [F_R_i = about three clutches annually], a high frequency that, when combined with the four-egg clutch size, yields a substantial annual reproductive output. This sustained multi-brooded strategy is energetically demanding, and the maximum reproductive rate is constrained by the time required for incubation, brooding, and post-fledging care of each brood. Comparative data from related cardueline finches suggest that the House finch's combination of modest clutch size with high brood frequency represents an adaptation to unpredictable resource availability across its expansive North American range, allowing rapid population recovery following periods of environmental stress.
